 WICHITA, Kan. (KAKE) — No charges will be filed against the driver in the Stryker Sports Complex crash, the Sedgwick County district attorney announced Thursday.
 “This is not a crime, and I cannot charge this driver with a crime,” Marc Bennett, Sedgwick County DA, said.
 Just after 3:45 p.m. on Thursday, the Wichita Police Department and Sedgwick County DA held a press conference to update the public on the Stryker Sports Complex Crash investigation.
 WPD Chief Joe Sullivan said before the incident, the driver of the truck involved told her children she was going to take a nap and put her seat all the way back. After she fell asleep, one of her children put up a sunshade.
 An off-duty officer observed the seat was all the way down after he approached the driver following the incident, Sullivan said.
 The driver was cooperative at all times, Sullivan said, and no impairing substances were found in the truck or in the blood sample she provided.
 No recalls were found for her vehicle. An inspection of the vehicle showed no mechanical issues. Police recreated the scene with an officer of a similar size and stature. Officers found that if the truck was left in drive, it would not go over the curb — meaning the gas had to have been engaged.
 Marc Bennett said a medical emergency had no role in the incident and there is no evidence of impairment.
 She was driving a truck that was not her normal vehicle from Garden City to Wichita, leaving at around 7 a.m.
 She parked in a west-facing stall that had a direct line onto the field. Her 14-year-old child put up a sunshade for her while she slept. The sideline was right in front of her truck — where her other child was.
 No evidence of an intentional crime — firm evidence that this was not intentional. No one at Stryker, Bennett said, had a problem with the driver.
 “If she was asleep with the car in park and somehow inadvertently, while she was sleeping, the car was thrown into gear. I don't have a mental state. There was no crime there,” Bennett said. “… There is no path forward to a criminal culpability for her. The only consideration that I have is if she left it in park.”
 Bennett said he needed to determine whether this was intentional or knowing.
 “There's not a lot of difference between an intentional act and a knowing act, but it means the person, the nature of the person's conduct that they knew or had knowledge of the nature of their conduct, and that they were aware of the nature of their conduct,” he said. “… I'll give you the ones of the people who were there. She was sleepy; looked like she'd just woken up. These are comments from witnesses who arrived there at the door and interacted with her.”
 The final means of culpability, Bennett said, as defined by Kansas law, is reckless.
 “A person acts recklessly or is reckless when [a] person consciously disregards a substantial and unjustifiable risk that circumstances exist. … They have to be aware of the circumstances and disregard the same.”
 Bennett said the driver said: “I put it in park.”
 “But thinking she had put it in park and thinking it was okay to go to sleep, that's not a conscious disregard,” he said. “That's a mistake.”
 Kansas does not have negligent homicide. The only thing Bennett could charge is vehicular homicide, but he said there is “not enough” evidence for it.
 “Vehicular homicide is defined by the killing of [a] human being committed while operating an airplane, automobile, motorboat, etc., in a manner which creates an unreasonable risk of injury to another person or property of another, and which constitutes a material deviation from the standard of care.”
 Bennett said that if he charged this, he would be guilty of hindsight bias.
 “There are no facts uncovered by this investigation to suggest this was an intentional act. There are no facts to conclude that this was a knowing act,” Bennett said. “There are no facts in this case uncovered to conclude that this was a reckless act, as that term is defined by Kansas law, not as understood in common parlance as we talk about it in our daily lives. But conscious disregard. I cannot prove she consciously disregarded a tremendous risk to the people on that field.”
 Sullivan said every available lead was pursued in this investigation.

 WICHITA, Kan. (KAKE) — Nearly a month has passed since police said a woman drove her truck into a youth soccer game at Stryker Sports Complex in northeast Wichita, killing two and injuring 10 others. On Thursday, the Wichita Police Department and Sedgwick County district attorney will hold a press conference to provide an update on the investigation.
 The conference is now scheduled for 3:45 p.m. Watch it on the player above, on KAKE's Facebook page or YouTube channel . 
 On Saturday, Oct. 17, at approximately 3:25 p.m., Sedgwick County Emergency Communications received multiple 911 calls reporting that a truck had driven onto a soccer field during a match at 29th and Greenwich in northeast Wichita. 
 Cole Adrian (left) and Nick Schafer
 Family photo/GoFundMe 
 Cole Adrian , 6, and Nicholas Schafer , 35, both from McPherson , were killed, and 10 others, ranging in age from 5 to 68, were injured and transported to area hospitals. Police have not provided updates on their conditions despite multiple requests from KAKE News.

 Police said the driver was identified as a 34-year-old woman from Garden City. Police said the woman “continues to cooperate with investigators” and was released from custody. The police department said that the woman’s release from custody does not represent a final determination about whether criminal charges are appropriate .

 After consulting with the Sedgwick County District Attorney’s Office , investigators did not have probable cause to arrest the driver, the police department said. Nearly 50 interviews with witnesses and others were conducted following the incident. Investigators are also inspecting the truck involved, analyzing available vehicle data.
 Video shows the moments before a woman driving a truck plowed through a soccer game at Stryker Sports Complex on Saturday afternoon.
